Here’s a hypothetical therapy scenario with a detailed backstory, followed by 100 distinct things the client might say during a session.

## Client backstory

The client is **Maya Thompson**, a **34-year-old middle school English teacher** living in a small apartment in **Portland, Oregon** with her senior rescue dog, **Juniper**. For most of her adult life, Maya has been known by friends and coworkers as dependable, thoughtful, and high-achieving. She was raised in a family where emotional expression was discouraged; her father was practical and critical, and her mother tended to avoid conflict by minimizing distress. Maya learned early to appear “fine” even when she felt overwhelmed.

Over the past year, Maya’s mental health has worsened significantly. About **10 months ago**, her **seven-year relationship ended** when her partner moved out unexpectedly after months of tension and emotional distance. Around the same time, Maya’s school underwent budget cuts, increasing her workload and leaving her responsible for larger class sizes and more administrative duties. She has also been helping care for her mother, who recently developed mobility problems, while feeling guilt that she is not doing “enough.”

Maya has struggled increasingly with **depression and anxiety**. She has trouble sleeping, often waking at **3:30 a.m.** with racing thoughts about work, money, and whether she is “falling behind in life.” Her appetite fluctuates. She finds it hard to enjoy things she used to love, like reading novels, baking, or taking Juniper on long walks through Forest Park. She has become socially withdrawn, ignores texts from close friends, and often cries in her car before work. She worries constantly that she is disappointing everyone and has begun to fear that she is fundamentally broken.

Today, Maya is meeting with her psychiatrist during a therapy-focused appointment and trying, somewhat reluctantly, to describe what’s been happening.

## 100 distinct statements the client might say

1. “I feel like I’ve been moving through wet cement for the last few months.”
2. “I’m exhausted all the time, but when I lie down at night, my brain won’t shut off.”
3. “I keep waking up around 3:30 in the morning and immediately thinking about everything I’m failing at.”
4. “It’s not just sadness—it feels heavier than that, like something is pressing down on me all day.”
5. “I used to love teaching literature, and now even planning a simple lesson feels impossible.”
6. “I cry in the parking lot before work more often than I want to admit.”
7. “I’m anxious from the moment I open my eyes.”
8. “I feel guilty all the time, even when I’m doing my best.”
9. “My friends keep checking in, and I ignore their texts because I don’t know how to explain any of this.”
10. “I cancel plans because I’m tired, but then I feel lonely and ashamed for canceling.”
11. “It feels like everyone else knows how to be an adult, and I’m just pretending.”
12. “Since the breakup, I haven’t really felt like myself.”
13. “I still expect to hear my ex come through the door sometimes, which makes me feel ridiculous.”
14. “I replay the end of the relationship constantly and keep wondering what I did wrong.”
15. “Part of me knows the breakup wasn’t entirely my fault, but emotionally it feels like it was.”
16. “I’ve stopped doing a lot of the things that used to make me feel grounded.”
17. “Even taking Juniper for a short walk feels like a huge effort some days.”
18. “I used to read every night, and now I can’t focus on more than a page or two.”
19. “My concentration is terrible; I keep rereading emails and still missing things.”
20. “I’m terrified people at work are starting to notice that I’m barely holding it together.”
21. “When my principal emails me, I get this immediate rush of panic.”
22. “I’m behind on grading, and every day I’m more behind, which makes me avoid it even more.”
23. “The anxiety makes me procrastinate, and then the procrastination makes me more anxious.”
24. “I feel trapped in that cycle.”
25. “My apartment is messier than it’s ever been, and I hate that it’s become a reflection of how I feel.”
26. “I stand in the kitchen staring at the fridge because I can’t decide what to eat.”
27. “Sometimes I forget to eat until late afternoon, and then I wonder why I feel shaky and overwhelmed.”
28. “Other times I just snack mindlessly because I need something to distract me.”
29. “I don’t feel excited about anything right now.”
30. “Things that should feel good barely register.”
31. “I know Juniper needs me, and honestly, she’s one of the main reasons I keep any routine at all.”
32. “I’m embarrassed by how hard basic tasks have become.”
33. “Showering feels like a chore I have to talk myself into.”
34. “Laundry has piled up because I keep telling myself I’ll do it tomorrow.”
35. “I’m so hard on myself that even resting feels like I’m doing something wrong.”
36. “If I sit down for an hour, I start hearing this voice in my head telling me I’m lazy.”
37. “I think a lot of this comes from how I grew up—nothing was ever quite good enough.”
38. “My dad always focused on what I could have done better.”
39. “I learned to look competent even when I was upset.”
40. “I don’t actually know how to ask for help without feeling weak.”
41. “When people ask how I’m doing, I automatically say ‘fine’ before I even think about it.”
42. “I’ve gotten so used to minimizing things that I’m not sure anyone understands how bad it feels.”
43. “I keep telling myself I should be able to handle this on my own.”
44. “Part of me is angry that I even need help.”
45. “Another part of me is relieved to finally say this out loud.”
46. “I worry that if I start crying, I won’t be able to stop.”
47. “I feel like I’m grieving multiple things at once.”
48. “I’m grieving the relationship, but also the version of myself I used to be.”
49. “It scares me how disconnected I feel from my old life.”
50. “I used to make plans for the future, and now it’s hard to picture next month.”
51. “Every small decision feels loaded, like I might choose wrong and make everything worse.”
52. “Even replying to an email can make my chest tighten.”
53. “Sometimes my heart starts pounding for no obvious reason.”
54. “I get this knot in my stomach on Sunday afternoons just thinking about Monday.”
55. “I’m tense all the time, like my body forgot how to relax.”
56. “I clench my jaw so much that I wake up with headaches.”
57. “I feel guilty that my students aren’t getting the best version of me.”
58. “I worry I’m letting them down.”
59. “I also worry I’m letting my mom down because I’m resentful about how much caregiving I’m doing.”
60. “Then I feel horrible for feeling resentful.”
61. “My mom asks for help a lot, and I don’t know how to set boundaries without feeling selfish.”
62. “I’m carrying so much resentment and guilt at the same time.”
63. “I keep comparing myself to people who seem to manage work, family, and relationships without falling apart.”
64. “I know social media probably makes that worse, but I still scroll when I’m feeling bad.”
65. “I look at everyone else’s lives and feel like I missed some class on how to be okay.”
66. “I’m lonely, but I also don’t want to be around people.”
67. “Being around people feels draining because I have to pretend.”
68. “When I’m alone too long, my thoughts get darker and more critical.”
69. “I feel stuck between wanting comfort and wanting to hide.”
70. “Sometimes I think I’ve become boring because all I talk about in my head is work, stress, and failure.”
71. “I’ve started assuming people are disappointed in me, even when they haven’t said anything.”
72. “If someone’s tone changes slightly, I immediately think I did something wrong.”
73. “I’m always scanning for signs that I’m in trouble.”
74. “It’s hard for me to tell the difference between a real problem and my anxiety filling in the blanks.”
75. “I know some of my thoughts are irrational, but they still feel convincing.”
76. “I keep waiting for a point where things finally feel manageable again.”
77. “I’m scared this is just who I am now.”
78. “I don’t want to keep living like this.”
79. “I want relief, even just a little bit.”
80. “I miss feeling present.”
81. “I miss laughing without forcing it.”
82. “I miss having energy to care about things.”
83. “I’ve been avoiding opening bills because money stress makes me panic.”
84. “I’m not in immediate danger, but I do feel overwhelmed by how relentless all of this is.”
85. “There are moments when I wonder if anything is ever going to get better.”
86. “That thought scares me, because I don’t want to feel hopeless.”
87. “I think I’ve spent so long functioning on anxiety that I don’t know what normal feels like.”
88. “When I’m not worrying, I almost feel guilty, like I’m forgetting something important.”
89. “I can’t remember the last time my body felt calm.”
90. “I’ve started dreading evenings because that’s when the loneliness really hits.”
91. “The apartment feels too quiet now.”
92. “Sometimes I leave the TV on just so it doesn’t feel so empty.”
93. “I keep thinking I should be ‘over’ the breakup by now, and then I judge myself for still hurting.”
94. “I’m angry at my ex, but mostly I’m angry at myself for not seeing things clearly sooner.”
95. “It’s hard for me to trust my own judgment right now.”
96. “I want to learn how to stop attacking myself for every mistake.”
97. “I want tools for the anxiety because I can’t keep living in this constant state of alarm.”
98. “I want to understand whether this is depression, burnout, grief, or all of it together.”
99. “I’m tired of surviving the day and then starting over again.”
100. “I really do want to feel better—I just don’t know how to get there from here.”

If you want, I can also turn this into:
- a more realistic **dialogue format** between client and psychiatrist,
- a version with a different **age/background/personality**,
- or a list focused specifically on **depression symptoms**, **anxiety symptoms**, or **trauma-related themes**.
